Why CO₂ is especially important in backend 
UPW has extremely high resistivity:
UPW ≈ 18.2 MΩ·cm → extremely poor electrical conductivity
During wafer dicing, grinding, high-pressure spraying, or spin rinsing, flowing UPW 
can generate electrostatic charge. This can cause electrostatic discharge (ESD) damage
to sensitive devices.
Adding a controlled amount of CO₂:
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌H₂CO₃ ⇌H⁺ + HCO₃⁻
increases ionic conductivity and therefore reduces water resistivity, allowing 
accumulated charge to dissipate.
Pure UPW → high resistivity → static charge risk
CO₂ + UPW → higher conductivity → lower static charge → ESD protection
This is why carbonated DI water / CO₂-DIW is particularly common around wafer dicing 
and some backend wet processes.

10. Forming Gas (FG) 
Forming gas is a controlled mixture of hydrogen (H₂) diluted in an inert gas, most commonly 
nitrogen (N₂). In semiconductor manufacturing, it is primarily used to create a mild reducing and 
passivating atmosphere during thermal treatment.
H₂ + N₂, commonly around 5–10% H₂ with balance N₂; exact concentration is fab/process 
dependent (e.g. H2/4.9%N2 FG or H2/4.9%Ar FG)
Why mix H₂ with N₂?
Pure H₂ is highly flammable and often provides more reducing capability than needed. Diluting it 
with N₂ gives a more controllable process atmosphere while retaining useful hydrogen chemistry.
The roles are essentially:
N₂ → dilution + inert carrier/protective atmosphere
H₂ → reduction + hydrogen passivation
The most important semiconductor mechanism is hydrogen passivation.
At a Si/SiO₂ interface, structural imperfections can leave unsatisfied Si bonds, often represented 
conceptually as: Si• + H → Si–H
Hydrogen terminates these dangling bonds, reducing electrically active interface traps.

Fundamental Principles of Plasma Etching 
A material can be etched efficiently only if the surface reaction produces a by-product that can 
leave the wafer surface under the process conditions.
Etchant species + wafer material → volatile reaction product → desorption → vacuum pump
If the product is nonvolatile, it stays on the surface, causing residue, micromasking, roughness, 
etch stop, or requiring stronger ion bombardment / higher temperature.
1. Silicon etched with ﬂuorine: Si(s) + 4F• → SiF₄(g)
SiF₄ is highly volatile, so it readily leaves the wafer.
Therefore: F radical → reacts with Si → SiF₄ gas → pumped away
This is why fluorine chemistry can produce a very high Si etch rate.
2. If Material + Etchant → nonvolatile solid
the product remains on the wafer:
Reaction → surface residue → blocks fresh etchant → etch slows/stops
Thus, selecting F, Cl, or Br is partly about asking:
Which halogen forms the most removable product with the material I want to etch?

Ar plasma → Ar⁺ → physical sputtering
When Ar enters the plasma: Ar + e⁻ → Ar⁺ + 2e⁻
The positively charged Ar⁺ ions are accelerated across the plasma sheath toward the wafer.

The ions transfer momentum to surface atoms:
Ar⁺ + Surface → momentum transfer → surface atom/product ejection
This is called sputtering or physical etching.
Unlike F, Cl or Br: F• + Si → SiF₄↑= chemical etching
whereas: Ar⁺ + Si → Si atom ejected = physical sputtering
Chemical reaction + Ar⁺ bombardment → ion-assisted chemical etching
Reactive gas + Ar
This is usually more powerful:
Chemical reaction + Ar⁺ bombardment → ion-assisted chemical etching
For example: Cl₂ + Ar
Cl radicals chemically react with the material while Ar⁺ helps break bonds and remove
